Common Questions

#### ADU FAQ

Utah ADU laws have changed a lot recently. Here's what most homeowners ask us first.

 Is an ADU legal on my Utah property?▼

In most Utah cities, yes. Since HB 82 (2021), internal ADUs like basement apartments are a permitted use in residential zones. And as of Oct. 1, 2026, SB 284 requires most larger Utah cities to allow a detached backyard ADU as a permitted use on single-family lots of 11,000 sq ft or more, with capped parking and no conditional use permit. Many cities allow detached ADUs on smaller lots too. We'll confirm your specific zoning during your free site visit, at no charge. Read our SB284 guide or check your lot.

 How do I get an estimate? Is it really free?▼

100% free, no strings attached. Just fill out the form on this page and we'll reach out within 1 business day to schedule a time to visit your property, walk through your options, and give you a clear picture of what's possible. You decide what happens next.

 What's the difference between stickbuilt, modular, and a garage conversion?▼

A stickbuilt ADU is built on-site from scratch: maximum customization, best long-term value. A modular ADU is built in a factory and assembled on your lot, faster and often more affordable. A garage conversion turns your existing garage into a fully livable, permitted unit, typically the most cost-effective option if you already have a usable garage.

 Can I rent out my ADU for extra income?▼

Yes, many of our clients build ADUs specifically to generate rental income. Long-term rentals are allowed anywhere ADUs are permitted in Utah. Short-term rentals (Airbnb, VRBO) depend on your city's specific rules. We can help you understand what's allowed in your area during your free consultation.

 How long does it take to build an ADU?▼

Garage conversions can be completed in as little as 2-3 months. Modular ADUs typically take 3-5 months from permit approval. Custom stickbuilt ADUs usually run 5-8 months. Permitting timelines vary by city (usually 4-10 weeks) and we manage all of that for you.

 Do I need to live on the property?▼

Utah doesn't have one statewide owner-occupancy rule, but state law lets cities require it: a city can prohibit renting an internal ADU in a home that isn't the owner's primary residence, and under SB284 (2026) a city can require the owner to live in either the main home or a detached ADU. Many cities do. We'll confirm the rule for your specific city as part of your free estimate.

 Do you handle permits and inspections?▼

Absolutely, that's one of the biggest things we do for you. We handle architectural plans, permit applications, utility hookups, all required inspections, and the final certificate of occupancy. You won't have to deal with city hall at all.

 Can you convert my garage even if it's attached to the house?▼

Yes, both attached and detached garages can often be converted into legal ADUs. We'll assess your garage's size, structure, and zoning situation during your free site visit to confirm feasibility and walk you through what the conversion would involve.

## Utah's New Detached ADU Law (SB284), Explained
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-utah-detached-adu-law-sb284-2026.html

New Utah Law

### Utah's New Detached ADU Law (SB284): What Changed Oct. 1, 2026

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- As of October 1, 2026, most larger Utah cities must allow a detached backyard ADU as a permitted use on single-family lots of 11,000 sq ft or more (Utah Code 10-21-304, created by SB284).

- Cities can no longer require a conditional use permit for a detached ADU in residential zones, and parking is capped at 2 spaces (650+ sq ft units) or 1 space (smaller units).

- Cities must also create a process to convert a legally built garage, shop, or other accessory building into a detached ADU.

- Cities can still regulate size, height, setbacks, lot coverage, owner occupancy, and short-term rentals (under 90 days), and your HOA can still say no to a detached unit.

For years, building a backyard cottage in Utah depended almost entirely on which city you lived in. Some cities allowed detached ADUs broadly, some only in small overlay zones, and some not at all. In 2026 the Legislature changed that. SB284, "Local Land and Water Modifications," sponsored by Sen. Lincoln Fillmore and Rep. Jill Koford, created a new section of state law, Utah Code 10-21-304, that makes detached ADUs a by-right use on qualifying lots in most of the state's larger cities. Cities had until October 1, 2026 to update their ordinances.

If you've been told "no" before, or never checked because you assumed your city didn't allow it, this is worth a second look. Here's exactly what changed, in plain English.

#### What Changed on October 1, 2026

Under Utah Code 10-21-304, a covered city must adopt rules that permit a detached accessory dwelling unit on any lot or parcel of 11,000 square feet or larger that contains a single-family home, as long as the single-family home is a permitted use on that lot. Cities are free to allow detached ADUs on smaller lots too. 11,000 sq ft is the ceiling a city can set as its minimum, not the floor.

For reference, 11,000 square feet is about a quarter acre (0.25 acres is 10,890 sq ft, so a lot needs to be just over a quarter acre). That describes a large share of older Wasatch Front neighborhoods and foothill subdivisions.

Every detached ADU still has to meet building, health, and fire codes, and the city's rules must include a path for owners of a legally built accessory structure (like a detached garage or workshop) to convert it into a detached ADU, subject to setbacks and code.

📐

Not sure how big your lot is? Answer 6 quick questions and we'll tell you which ADU options your property likely qualifies for. We'll look up your parcel for free.Check My Lot →

#### Which Cities the Law Covers

SB284 applies to what state code calls a "specified municipality": the cities required to adopt a detailed moderate-income housing plan. In practice that means first- through fourth-class cities, plus fifth-class cities with 5,000 or more residents in the state's larger counties. That includes most of the cities along the Wasatch Front: places like Salt Lake City, Sandy, West Jordan, Orem, Provo, Lehi, Layton, and Ogden.

Small towns and unincorporated county areas may not be covered by the mandate, although many (Salt Lake County's unincorporated areas, for example) have their own ADU ordinances. If you're unsure whether your city is covered, ask us. Checking is part of our free site visit.

#### What Cities Can No Longer Require

For a detached ADU in a covered city, the city's ordinance may not:

- Require a conditional use permit if the ADU is in a primarily residential zone. Detached ADUs are now a permitted use, which means an administrative approval instead of a discretionary hearing in front of a planning commission.

- Require more than two on-site parking spaces for a detached ADU that is 650 sq ft or larger.

- Require more than one on-site parking space for a detached ADU smaller than 650 sq ft.

- Impose design standards that conflict with the state's limits on residential design rules (Utah Code 10-20-618).

Parking minimums have quietly killed a lot of ADU projects. Provo, for example, has required four off-street spaces for a house and its ADU combined, a rule the new law overrides for detached units.

#### What Cities Can Still Regulate

SB284 isn't a free-for-all. A covered city may still:

- Apply its normal rules on size, dimensions, height, and maximum lot coverage, plus setbacks (which can consider property lines, other structures, easements, window placement, and massing).

- Require the ADU to be designed consistently with the main house.

- Prohibit a detached ADU that is larger than the main home, sits in the front yard, or sits in a utility or other recorded easement.

- Prohibit renting the detached ADU for fewer than 90 consecutive days, which effectively bans short-term rentals like Airbnb.

- Require the owner to live in either the main house or the ADU.

- Limit lots to one detached ADU.

- Require that parking lost in a detached garage conversion be replaced on-site.

- Deny a detached ADU where there isn't adequate sewer, culinary water, electrical, or storm water access or capacity.

The law also doesn't override restrictions in development agreements a city signed on or before May 6, 2026, so some newer master-planned subdivisions may still be off-limits.

💲

Qualify? Next question is cost. Get an instant ballpark for a detached, modular, or garage-conversion ADU based on real Utah project pricing.Try the ADU Cost Calculator →

#### How Utah Cities Are Responding

Because each city wrote its own ordinance within the state framework, the details vary a lot from city to city:

- Lehi previously allowed detached ADUs only on lots of 14,520 sq ft or more, capped at 1,300 sq ft. In July 2026 it lowered the minimum lot to 11,000 sq ft, required detached units to sit at least 6 feet from the house, and required owner occupancy of one of the two units. City staff estimated the number of eligible lots could grow by up to 20%.

- Orem had never allowed detached ADUs. Its new rules, adopted in September 2026, allow them on qualifying lots but limit them to one story and 20 feet, keep them out of front yards, and prohibit short-term rentals.

- Provo had limited detached ADUs to specific overlay zones. This fall it moved to allow them on qualifying 11,000+ sq ft lots citywide, with a draft allowing units up to 25 feet tall. Earlier proposals also discussed capping total accessory-structure coverage at 40% of the lot.

- Salt Lake City was ahead of the law. It already allows detached ADUs without the 11,000 sq ft threshold, up to 1,000 sq ft and no larger than the main building, with owner occupancy required and generally 3-foot side and rear setbacks.

- Sandy, Layton, Alpine, Lindon, and Vineyard were among the other cities adopting compliant ordinances in 2026, with their own height and setback details.

Because these ordinances are brand new, city staff and even some contractors are still learning them. The single most useful thing you can do is get a property-specific answer before you pay for plans.

#### Internal ADUs: The 2021 Rules Still Apply

SB284 is about detached units. Internal ADUs (a basement apartment or a unit within your home's footprint) are still governed by the rules that started with HB82 in 2021, now in Utah Code 10-21-303. In areas zoned primarily residential, an internal ADU is a permitted use, and cities generally can't regulate its size relative to the house, total lot size, or street frontage. Cities may:

- Require one additional on-site parking space (and replacement parking if the ADU takes over a garage or carport).

- Prohibit internal ADUs on lots of 6,000 sq ft or less, or where the home is on a failing septic tank.

- Prohibit rentals of fewer than 30 consecutive days.

- Prohibit renting an internal ADU if the home isn't the owner's primary residence.

- Require a rental permit or license, and prohibit a separate utility meter.

Cities that issue an ADU permit can also record a notice on the property, and can place a lien (up to $100/day after a cure period) for unresolved violations, which is one more reason not to build without a permit.

#### HOAs: The Big Exception

State ADU mandates apply to cities, not to private covenants. According to the Utah Department of Commerce's HOA office, an HOA can still prohibit detached ADUs even where state law and city ordinances allow them. HOAs generally cannot ban internal ADUs, though they can require them to meet zoning and building, health, and fire codes. If you're in an HOA, read your CC&Rs before anything else. Our HOA guide walks through what to look for.

#### Does Your Lot Qualify? A Quick Checklist

- Lot size: 11,000 sq ft or more is the magic number in most covered cities. Your county assessor's parcel lookup shows it, or we'll pull it for you.

- Zoning: the lot must hold a single-family home in a zone where single-family homes are permitted.

- Space: room behind or beside the house that meets setbacks and stays out of easements and the front yard.

- Utilities: reasonable access to sewer, water, and power. Distance is the biggest cost driver (see our utility hookup guide).

- Existing structure: a legally built detached garage or shop may now be convertible.

- HOA: no detached-ADU prohibition in your CC&Rs.

- Your plans: you're comfortable with owner-occupancy and long-term (90+ day) rental rules.

If you check most of these boxes, you're likely in a much better position than you were a year ago.

This guide summarizes Utah Code 10-21-304 and 10-21-303 and recent city actions as of November 2026. It's general information, not legal advice. City ordinances vary and continue to change, so confirm current rules with your city's planning department, and talk to an attorney about anything specific to your property or HOA.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

##### Can I build a backyard ADU in Utah?

In most Utah cities, yes. Internal ADUs (inside your home's footprint) have been a permitted use in residential zones since HB82 in 2021. As of Oct. 1, 2026, SB284 (Utah Code 10-21-304) also requires most larger Utah cities to allow a detached backyard ADU as a permitted use on single-family lots of 11,000 square feet or more. Cities may allow detached ADUs on smaller lots, and many already do.
##### Which Utah cities have to allow detached ADUs under SB284?

The law applies to 'specified municipalities' under Utah's moderate-income-housing statute: generally first- through fourth-class cities, plus fifth-class cities of 5,000 or more residents in the state's larger counties. That covers most cities along the Wasatch Front. Cities had to adopt compliant ordinances by Oct. 1, 2026.
##### How much parking can a Utah city require for a detached ADU?

Under SB284, a covered city cannot require more than two on-site parking spaces for a detached ADU of 650 square feet or larger, or more than one space for a detached ADU smaller than 650 square feet. If you convert a detached garage, the city can require you to replace the home's parking spaces that were in that garage.
##### Can I use a Utah ADU as an Airbnb?

Usually not. Under SB284, cities may prohibit renting a detached ADU for fewer than 90 consecutive days, and under the internal ADU statute cities may prohibit internal ADU rentals of fewer than 30 consecutive days. Most cities use these limits, so plan on long-term or mid-term rentals.
##### Do I have to live on the property to build an ADU in Utah?

Often, yes. SB284 lets cities require the owner to live in either the main house or the detached ADU, and the internal ADU statute lets cities prohibit renting an internal ADU in a home that is not the owner's primary residence. Lehi, Salt Lake City, and Salt Lake County all have owner-occupancy rules.
##### Can my HOA stop me from building a detached ADU in Utah?

Yes. According to the Utah Department of Commerce, an HOA can still prohibit detached ADUs even where state law and city ordinances allow them. HOAs generally cannot ban internal ADUs, but they can require them to meet zoning, building, health, and fire codes.

#### Sources

- Utah Code 10-21-304, Detached accessory dwelling units (effective 10/1/2026)

- Utah Code 10-21-303, Internal accessory dwelling units

- S.B. 284 (2026), Local Land and Water Modifications, enrolled copy

- Utah Department of Commerce, Accessory Dwelling Units and HOAs

- Deseret News, Provo ADU ordinance changes (Oct. 2026)

- Daily Herald, Utah County cities prepare for statewide detached ADU changes (July 2026)

#### How Utah's ADU rules work in 2026

Internal ADUs (inside your home's footprint, like a basement apartment) have been a permitted use in Utah's residential zones since 2021. Detached ADUs got a major boost on October 1, 2026, when SB284 began requiring most larger Utah cities to allow them as a permitted use on single-family lots of 11,000 sq ft or more, with capped parking and no conditional use permit. Cities can still regulate size, height, setbacks, owner occupancy, and short-term rentals, and HOAs can still prohibit detached units. ADU Pricing Guide

### How Much Does an ADU Cost in Utah?

Honest, straightforward pricing information so you can plan with confidence. Every project is different, but here is what you can generally expect to invest.

💲 Want a number for your property? Try the free ADU cost calculator →

Pricing Overview

#### ADU Cost Ranges in Utah

These ranges reflect real project costs in Utah based on current material and labor prices. Your exact cost depends on your lot, the model you choose, finishes, and site conditions. A free property visit gives you the most accurate number.

🚗

##### Garage Conversion ADU

Typical Range

$50K - $120K

The most affordable path to a legal ADU. You're working with an existing structure, which eliminates foundation and framing costs. Great for homeowners who want rental income without a large upfront investment.

- Uses your existing garage structure

- Lower cost than new construction

- Full electrical, plumbing and insulation included

- Permits and inspections handled

- Best ROI for budget-conscious homeowners

Most Common

🏗️

##### Prefab / Modular ADU

Typical Range

$120K - $200K

Factory-built and assembled on your lot. Faster to complete and generally more cost-effective than full custom builds. A great balance of quality, speed, and value for most Utah homeowners.

- Studio, 1 bed and 2 bed models available

- Built to the same code as stickbuilt

- 50 to 70% faster than traditional construction

- Foundation, delivery and set included

- Permits and inspections handled

🏠

##### Custom Stickbuilt ADU

Typical Range

$120K - $300K

Built on-site from the ground up with full customization. Maximum design flexibility, premium finishes, and the highest long-term property value. Ideal for homeowners who want something completely tailored to their lot and style.

- Fully custom floor plans and layouts

- Your choice of finishes and materials

- Matches your home's architecture

- Highest resale and rental value

- Studio up to 3 bedrooms available

 Important Note on Pricing
 These ranges are general estimates based on current Utah market conditions. Your actual cost will depend on your specific lot, local permitting fees, site preparation needs, utility hookups, and the finishes you choose. The only way to get an accurate number for your property is a free site visit. We will give you a straight, honest estimate with no pressure.

Cost Factors

#### What Affects the Final Price

No two ADU projects are identical. Here are the main factors that move the needle on cost.

📐

###### Size and Square Footage

Larger units cost more to build. A 400 sq ft studio will always come in lower than a 900 sq ft 2-bedroom. That said, cost per square foot actually decreases as you go bigger.

🏗️

###### Build Type

Modular ADUs are faster and typically less expensive than custom stickbuilt. Garage conversions are the most affordable since you're working with an existing structure. See our modular vs. stickbuilt comparison for a full breakdown.

🔧

###### Site Preparation

Sloped lots, poor soil conditions, or limited access can add to site prep costs. Flat, accessible lots with easy utility connections cost less to develop.

✨

###### Finishes and Materials

Standard finishes are included in base pricing. Upgraded flooring, custom cabinetry, premium appliances, and high-end fixtures can add $10K to $40K depending on selections.

📋

###### Permits and Fees

City permit fees in Utah typically range from $3,000 to $12,000 depending on the municipality. We handle all permitting and these fees are included in your estimate. Rules vary by city — see our Utah ADU law guide for details.

💡

###### Utility Connections

Connecting to existing water, sewer, gas, and electrical can vary significantly depending on how far your ADU is from the main home and existing infrastructure.

Return on Investment

#### ADUs Are One of the Best Investments You Can Make

When you look at the numbers, a well-built ADU pays for itself — and then some. Here is what Utah homeowners are seeing.

 $1,200 - $2,500

###### Monthly Rental Income

Depending on size, location, and finishes, Utah ADUs are renting for strong numbers in 2026 especially in Salt Lake City and Park City.

 5 - 10 Years

###### Average Payback Period

Most ADU owners recoup their full investment through rental income within 5 to 10 years. After that it is pure profit every month.

 20 - 30%

###### Property Value Increase

A finished, permitted ADU adds significant value to your home beyond just the rental income. Buyers pay a premium for properties with ADUs.

Common Questions

#### Pricing FAQ

What affects the final price of an ADU in Utah? +

The main factors are size and square footage, build type (garage conversion, modular, or custom stickbuilt), site preparation needs, finishes and materials, permit fees (typically $3,000 to $12,000 depending on the municipality), and utility connection costs. A free site visit gives you the most accurate number for your specific property.

What kind of return can I expect on an ADU in Utah? +

Utah ADUs are renting for roughly $1,200 to $2,500 a month depending on size, location, and finishes, especially in Salt Lake City and Park City. Most owners recoup their investment through rental income within 5 to 10 years, and a finished, permitted ADU can add 20 to 30% to a home's value on top of the rental income.

Which ADU type costs the least in Utah? +

A garage conversion is typically the most affordable, ranging from $50,000 to $120,000, since you're working with an existing structure and avoiding foundation and framing costs. Modular ADUs run $120,000 to $200,000, and custom stickbuilt ADUs run $120,000 to $300,000.

## ADU Financing Options | Utah Backyard ADUs
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/financing.html

ADU Financing Guide

### How to Finance Your ADU

You don't have to pay cash upfront. Most homeowners use equity they already have in their home to fund their ADU build. Here's how it works.

Your Options

#### The Most Common Ways to Finance an ADU

If you own your home and have built up equity over the years, you likely have more financing options than you realize. Here are the four most popular paths Utah homeowners use to fund their ADU projects.

🏦

Most Popular

##### HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit)

A HELOC works like a credit card backed by your home equity. You're approved for a credit limit and draw funds as you need them during construction. You only pay interest on what you actually use.

Typical RatePrime + 0 to 2% (variable)

Draw Period5 to 10 years

Repayment10 to 20 years after draw

Typical LimitUp to 85% of home equity

Only pay interest on what you draw

Reusable credit line during draw period

Flexible for phased projects

Variable rate can rise over time

💰

Fixed Payments

##### Home Equity Loan (Second Mortgage)

A home equity loan gives you one lump sum upfront at a fixed interest rate. Your monthly payment stays the same for the life of the loan, making it easy to budget. Great for homeowners who want predictability.

Typical RateFixed, varies by lender

Loan Term5 to 30 years

DisbursementSingle lump sum at closing

Typical LimitUp to 85% of home equity

Fixed rate, predictable payments

Simple one-time disbursement

You pay interest on full amount immediately

Less flexible than a HELOC

🔄

Refinance Option

##### Cash-Out Refinance

You replace your existing mortgage with a new, larger mortgage and take the difference in cash. Works well if current rates are favorable or you have a high-rate existing mortgage. Rolls everything into one payment.

Typical RateCurrent mortgage rates

Max Cash OutUp to 80% of home value

Loan Term15 or 30 years

Closing Costs2% to 5% of loan amount

Single monthly payment

Potentially lowest rate if timed right

Resets mortgage term and closing costs

Not ideal if current rate is low

🏗️

Build-to-Perm

##### Construction Loan / ADU Loan

Construction loans are specifically designed for building projects. Funds are released in stages as construction milestones are hit. Some lenders now offer ADU-specific products with streamlined approval processes for projects under $250K.

Typical RateSlightly higher than mortgage rates

Draw ScheduleTied to construction milestones

Term12 to 18 months, then converts

Down PaymentTypically 20%+

Purpose-built for construction projects

Converts to permanent loan at completion

More paperwork and inspections required

Higher rate during construction phase

Understanding Equity

#### How Home Equity Works for ADU Financing

Most ADU financing is based on home equity. Here's a simple breakdown of how lenders calculate how much you can borrow.

##### What Is Home Equity?

Home equity is the portion of your home's value that you actually own. It's the difference between what your home is currently worth and what you still owe on your mortgage. The more equity you have, the more you can typically borrow for a project like an ADU.

Most lenders will let you borrow up to 80 to 85 percent of your home's appraised value, minus what you owe on your current mortgage. This is called your Combined Loan-to-Value (CLTV) ratio.

###### Example Calculation

Current Home Value$600,000

Lender Max CLTV (85%)$510,000

Remaining Mortgage Balance- $300,000

Available to Borrow$210,000

In this example, the homeowner could potentially access up to $210,000 to fund their ADU build. Actual amounts depend on credit score, income, and lender requirements.

Side by Side

#### Quick Comparison

Every financing option has tradeoffs. Here is a quick breakdown to help you decide which direction to explore first.

 Option
 Rate Type
 Best For
 Complexity

 | HELOC Most Flexible
 | Variable
 | Phased builds, flexibility
 | Low to Medium

 | Home Equity Loan
 | Fixed
 | Predictable budgets
 | Low

 | Cash-Out Refinance
 | Fixed
 | High equity, favorable rates
 | Medium

 | Construction Loan
 | Variable then Fixed
 | New builds without equity
 | High

Pro Tips

#### Before You Apply for Financing

A little preparation before you walk into a bank can save you thousands. Here are the most important things to get right.

01

###### Know Your Credit Score

Most equity-based loans require a credit score of 620 or above. Scores above 720 get the best rates. Pull your free report at annualcreditreport.com before applying.

02

###### Get a Real Estimate First

Lenders want to know what you're borrowing for. Having a detailed written estimate from a licensed contractor makes your application stronger and avoids over-borrowing. See our full ADU cost breakdown to get a ballpark before you apply.

03

###### Shop Multiple Lenders

HELOC and home equity loan rates vary significantly between banks and credit unions. Getting 3 or more quotes can save you a full percentage point or more on your rate.

04

###### Factor In All Costs

Your loan amount should cover construction, permits, utility connections, landscaping, and a 10 to 15 percent contingency buffer. Surprises happen in construction.

05

###### Consider the Rental Math

A $150,000 ADU financed at 7% over 20 years costs about $1,160 per month. If you rent for $1,500 to $2,000 per month, the unit pays for itself and generates positive cash flow.

06

###### Check with Local Credit Unions

Utah credit unions often have better HELOC and home equity loan rates than big banks. America First, Mountain America, and Utah Power Credit Union are worth checking.

Common Questions

#### Financing FAQs

Can I finance an ADU if I still have a mortgage? +

Yes. Having an existing mortgage does not disqualify you. A HELOC or home equity loan sits on top of your primary mortgage as a second lien. You just need sufficient equity. Most lenders allow combined borrowing up to 85% of your home's appraised value.

How much equity do I need to qualify? +

To borrow $150,000 to $200,000 for an ADU, you generally need at least $200,000 to $250,000 in usable equity after your existing mortgage balance. Homes in the Wasatch Front have seen strong appreciation, so many homeowners have more equity than they realize.

Does an ADU increase my home's appraised value? +

Yes, in most cases. A properly permitted ADU adds rentable square footage and income potential, both of which appraisers factor in. Many Utah homeowners see their home value increase by 20 to 30 percent after adding an ADU, which can also free up more equity for future projects.

How long does it take to get approved for a HELOC? +

HELOC approvals typically take 2 to 6 weeks from application to funding. This includes a home appraisal, underwriting, and closing. Starting your financing process early, before construction begins, keeps your project on schedule.

Is the interest on a HELOC or home equity loan tax deductible? +

Interest may be deductible if the loan is used to substantially improve your home. An ADU generally qualifies as a home improvement. Consult a tax professional to confirm how current tax law applies to your specific situation, as rules can change.

What if I don't have enough equity? +

If your equity is limited, a construction loan or ADU-specific loan product may still be available to you. Some lenders offer loans based on the projected after-renovation value of your property. A garage conversion at $50,000 to $120,000 may also be achievable with a personal loan or smaller HELOC.

Local Requirements

#### What Salt Lake City Requires for an ADU

Every Utah city sets its own rules for accessory dwelling units on top of state law. Here's what matters most for Salt Lake City properties.

📏
###### Size Limits

Detached ADUs are capped at 1,000 sq ft in Salt Lake City. There's no size cap if you build an internal ADU inside your existing home instead.

🚗
###### Parking

Most Salt Lake City neighborhoods require one off-street parking space per ADU — though homes near a TRAX stop or UTA bus route may qualify for a waiver.

🏡
###### Owner-Occupancy

Salt Lake City requires that either your main home or your ADU be your primary residence, and short-term rentals like Airbnb aren't allowed on ADUs here.

Ordinances change and every lot is different — we confirm your exact zoning, setbacks, and options during your free site visit, at no cost.

## Aging in Place: Designing an ADU for Multigenerational Living
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-aging-in-place-multigenerational.html

ADU Guide

### Aging in Place: Designing an ADU for Multigenerational Living

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Rising home prices along the Wasatch Front have made multigenerational living a practical choice, not just a cultural preference, for a lot of families.
- It's worth clarifying a common point of confusion: the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) technically applies to public accommodations and commercial spaces, not private single-family homes.

A growing share of the ADUs we build aren't for rental income at all, they're for family: aging parents who want independence without distance, adult children saving toward their own home, or households simply choosing to live near each other by design. Building for this purpose well requires some different thinking than a standard rental unit.

#### Why Utah Families Are Building Multigenerational ADUs

Rising home prices along the Wasatch Front have made multigenerational living a practical choice, not just a cultural preference, for a lot of families. An ADU offers something a shared house often can't: real privacy and independence for both households, while keeping everyone on the same property for caregiving, childcare, or simply staying close.

#### Design Features That Matter Most

If aging in place is a real consideration, even years down the road, a handful of design choices are far easier to build in from day one than to retrofit later:

- Zero-step entry — no stairs at the main entrance, which matters immediately for wheelchair or walker access and eventually for anyone with mobility changes

- Wider doorways and hallways — 36-inch doorways and adequately wide hallways accommodate mobility devices without a future remodel

- Roll-in or curbless showers — far easier and cheaper to build correctly the first time than to retrofit a standard tub-shower combo later

- Lever-style door handles and single-lever faucets — small details that matter a lot for anyone with limited grip strength

- Single-story layout — most ADUs are single story by nature, which is itself one of the biggest aging-in-place advantages over a multi-level home

- Good lighting and slip-resistant flooring — especially in bathrooms and entryways

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### Universal Design vs. Full ADA Compliance

It's worth clarifying a common point of confusion: the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) technically applies to public accommodations and commercial spaces, not private single-family homes. What most homeowners actually want is "universal design," a set of best practices borrowed from accessibility standards that make a home more comfortable and usable for people of all ages and ability levels, without necessarily meeting the full technical requirements of commercial ADA compliance. In practice, this gives you flexibility to prioritize the features that matter most for your specific family rather than checking every box on a commercial accessibility code.

#### Planning for the Future, Not Just Today

The families who are happiest with their multigenerational ADU years later are usually the ones who designed a little ahead of their immediate needs: a parent who's independent and mobile today but chose a zero-step entry anyway, or a family that built a wider bathroom doorway "just in case" long before it was actually needed. These choices add very little to the cost during initial construction and are dramatically more expensive to add after the fact.

If a multigenerational or aging-in-place ADU is what you're considering, we'll walk through exactly which of these features make sense for your specific family and property during your free site visit, no pressure to over-build or under-build for a future that may or may not arrive as expected.

## Can Your HOA Stop You From Building an ADU in Utah?
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-hoa-rules-utah.html

ADU Guide

### Can Your HOA Stop You From Building an ADU in Utah?

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published August 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Under the Utah Community Association Act (specifically sections 57-8a-209(10) and 57-8a-218(16)), an HOA cannot prohibit an internal accessory dwelling unit — a unit built inside your existing home, like a basement apartment or a converted attached space.
- A detached ADU — a standalone backyard unit, separate from the main house — is not protected the same way.
- If you're in an HOA, the CC&Rs (and any amendments) are the actual source of truth for your property — not a general summary like this one.

State law has made it easier than ever to build an ADU in Utah — but if your property is in a homeowners association, state law and your HOA's rules don't always say the same thing. The honest answer is: it depends on what kind of ADU you're building.

#### Internal ADUs: Your HOA Generally Can't Ban Them

Under the Utah Community Association Act (specifically sections 57-8a-209(10) and 57-8a-218(16)), an HOA cannot prohibit an internal accessory dwelling unit — a unit built inside your existing home, like a basement apartment or a converted attached space. This holds even if your HOA's governing documents contain an older, blanket ban on ADUs; state law overrides those provisions regardless of when they were written.

That doesn't mean an HOA has zero say. It can still require an internal ADU to comply with four objective standards:

- Local zoning and land use ordinances

- Building codes

- Health codes (sanitation, water access)

- Fire codes (egress, fire-rated separations)

Notably, an HOA generally can't stop you from renting out an internal ADU once it meets those codes — that decision belongs to the homeowner, not the association.

#### Detached ADUs: A Different Story

A detached ADU — a standalone backyard unit, separate from the main house — is not protected the same way. Under current Utah law, an HOA can prohibit detached ADUs on its properties, even in a city that otherwise allows and encourages them under HB82 or SB284. Most of what we build (custom stickbuilt and modular backyard units) falls into this detached category, so this is the question we get most often from homeowners in an HOA.

In practice, this means SB284's statewide push for cities to permit detached ADUs doesn't automatically open the door on your specific lot if your HOA's CC&Rs say otherwise. City approval and HOA approval are two separate hurdles, and you need to clear both.

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### What to Check Before You Design Anything

If you're in an HOA, the CC&Rs (and any amendments) are the actual source of truth for your property — not a general summary like this one. A few things worth doing before you invest in design work:

- Request a current copy of your CC&Rs and any ADU-specific amendments from your HOA board or management company

- Ask directly whether detached ADUs are addressed, and if so, what design review process applies

- If you're planning an internal ADU, confirm which of the four objective standards above (zoning, building, health, fire) your HOA is actually enforcing, so there are no surprises during permitting

We handle the city side of permitting on every project — zoning, plan review, and inspections — but your HOA relationship is yours, and it's worth resolving before we design around a lot that an HOA won't ultimately approve. We're glad to talk through what we're seeing on your specific address during a free site visit.

This article summarizes provisions of the Utah Community Association Act as a general starting point — it is not legal advice. HOA documents vary property to property, and the law can change. Read your specific CC&Rs and, if anything is unclear, talk to an attorney or your HOA's management company before you rely on this summary.

For the state and city-level rules that apply whether or not you're in an HOA, see our guide to Utah's ADU laws (HB82 and SB284).

## ADU Insurance: What Utah Homeowners Need to Know Before Renting It Out
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-insurance-guide.html

ADU Guide

### ADU Insurance: What Utah Homeowners Need to Know Before Renting It Out

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- If your ADU is used by family members — a parent, an adult child, a guest suite — it's typically covered under your existing homeowners policy, though you may need to increase your dwelling coverage limits to reflect the added square footage and rebuild cost.
- Once you're renting the unit out, you'll typically need a landlord (or "dwelling fire") policy specifically for the rented structure.

Insurance is one of the least glamorous parts of building an ADU, and also one of the easiest to get wrong. Here's a plain-English rundown of how coverage typically works, so you can have an informed conversation with your own insurance agent.

#### Your Homeowners Policy Covers It, Until You Rent It Out

If your ADU is used by family members — a parent, an adult child, a guest suite — it's typically covered under your existing homeowners policy, though you may need to increase your dwelling coverage limits to reflect the added square footage and rebuild cost. The moment you rent the unit to a non-family tenant, that changes. Most standard homeowners policies either exclude or sharply limit coverage for rented structures, which means a claim involving your tenant's unit could get denied entirely if you haven't updated your coverage.

#### Landlord Policies: DP-1, DP-2, and DP-3

Once you're renting the unit out, you'll typically need a landlord (or "dwelling fire") policy specifically for the rented structure. These come in three common tiers:

- DP-1 — basic, named-peril coverage (fire, lightning, and a limited list of other causes)

- DP-2 — broader named-peril coverage, more causes of loss included

- DP-3 — open-peril coverage, the most comprehensive of the three, covering all causes of loss except those specifically excluded

Which tier makes sense depends on your risk tolerance, the unit's value, and your budget — this is exactly the kind of decision to make with a licensed agent rather than guess at.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### What Landlord Insurance Actually Covers

Beyond basic property damage, a landlord policy typically covers damage caused by tenants (as opposed to the family-use assumption built into a standard homeowners policy), and often includes loss-of-rental-income coverage if the unit becomes uninhabitable and you can't collect rent while it's repaired. Liability coverage for tenant injuries on the property is another piece worth confirming explicitly rather than assuming it's included.

#### What It Typically Costs

Adding ADU coverage, whether as an endorsement to your existing policy or a separate landlord policy, commonly adds somewhere in the range of $200-$1,200 per year to your overall insurance costs, depending on the unit's construction cost, whether it's attached or detached, and the coverage limits you choose. Get a specific quote before you finalize your rental pricing math — it's a real number that affects your actual return.

#### Questions Worth Asking Your Agent

- Does my current policy cover the ADU as-is, or do I need an endorsement?

- At what point does renting it out require a separate landlord policy?

- Is loss-of-rental-income coverage included, or is it an add-on?

- Does the policy distinguish between long-term tenants and short-term (Airbnb-style) rentals?

- What's excluded, and does that change if the ADU is a garage conversion vs. a detached structure?

This article is for general education only and isn't insurance advice. Coverage rules, costs, and available policy types vary by insurer and by your specific situation — talk to a licensed insurance agent before making coverage decisions.

We're happy to walk through what type of structure your ADU will be (attached, detached, or garage conversion) so you have the right details to bring to your insurance conversation — that's part of what we cover during your free site visit.

Once you're insured and ready to find a tenant, see Renting Out Your ADU in Utah: A Landlord's Basics for the notice periods and disclosures Utah law requires.

## The ADU Permitting Process in Utah: A Step-by-Step Guide
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-permitting-process-utah.html

ADU Guide

### The ADU Permitting Process in Utah: A Step-by-Step Guide

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- We submit your complete application package to your city's building department: site plan, floor plans, elevations, structural details, and energy code compliance documentation.
- City plan reviewers check your submittal against the Utah Residential Code (Utah adopted the 2021 IRC statewide effective July 2023) plus any local amendments.

"How long does permitting take?" is one of the first questions almost every homeowner asks us, and it's a fair one — permitting is the part of the process you can't see and can't really control yourself. Here's exactly what happens, in order, from your first call to your final inspection.

#### Step 1: Free Site Visit & Zoning Check

Before anything gets designed, we walk your property and pull your lot's zoning designation, setbacks, and any overlay restrictions specific to your city. This is also when we confirm whether your city requires owner-occupancy (Salt Lake City, Provo, and Ogden still do) and what size cap applies to your lot. You can read city-specific detail on our Salt Lake City, Provo, Park City, and Ogden pages, or see our full breakdown of what's changed under HB82 and SB284.

#### Step 2: Design & Architectural Plans

Once we know what your lot allows, we move into design — either from one of our existing floor plans or a fully custom layout. For a stickbuilt or garage conversion, this means stamped architectural drawings ready for submittal. For a modular unit, the factory's engineering department handles plan development, and we coordinate the site-specific foundation and utility plans locally.

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### Step 3: Submitting the Permit Application

We submit your complete application package to your city's building department: site plan, floor plans, elevations, structural details, and energy code compliance documentation. Every Utah city we build in has slightly different submittal requirements and fee schedules, which is exactly why doing this yourself the first time is where most delays happen.

#### Step 4: Plan Review

City plan reviewers check your submittal against the Utah Residential Code (Utah adopted the 2021 IRC statewide effective July 2023) plus any local amendments. Review timelines run anywhere from a couple of weeks to a couple of months depending on the city and how busy their department is. If reviewers come back with comments or requested revisions, we handle the resubmittal, so you're never the one going back and forth with city staff.

#### Step 5: Construction & Required Inspections

Once your permit is issued, construction begins, and inspections happen at specific milestones. A typical Utah ADU project goes through inspections at these stages:

- Footings and foundation — before concrete is poured

- Underground plumbing and electrical — before the slab is closed up

- Framing — structure, sheathing, and connections

- Rough plumbing, electrical, and mechanical — before walls are closed

- Insulation — verifying energy code compliance

- Drywall / firewall — for units near property lines or shared walls

- Final inspection — the last check before occupancy

Missing or failing an inspection doesn't just cost time, it can mean opening up finished work to fix something a crew rushed past. We schedule and attend every one of these ourselves.

#### Step 6: Certificate of Occupancy

Once your final inspection passes, the city issues a certificate of occupancy, and the unit is legally ready to be lived in or rented. This is the document that protects you at resale, at refinance, and if you ever need to prove the unit was built legally.

#### What This Means for Your Timeline

Adding it all up: garage conversions typically move through this whole process in 2-3 months, modular ADUs in 3-5 months, and custom stickbuilt units in 5-8 months, with permitting itself usually accounting for 4-10 weeks of that depending on your city. See our full cost and timeline comparison in How Much Does an ADU Cost in Utah?

The honest truth is that permitting is the one part of this process a homeowner can't shortcut or DIY effectively. It's also the entire reason we exist as a founder-led company: we manage the plans, the submittal, the revisions, and every inspection so you're never the one calling city hall.

## ADU Tax Implications: Rental Income, Depreciation & Deductions
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-tax-implications.html

ADU Guide

### ADU Tax Implications: Rental Income, Depreciation & Deductions

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Rent you collect from an ADU tenant is taxable income, reported similarly to any other residential rental property.
- Residential rental property is generally depreciated over 27.5 years under the standard MACRS schedule.
- Some ADU owners use a cost segregation study to reclassify certain components of construction cost (specific finishes, fixtures, or systems) into shorter depreciation categories, allowing a larger deduction sooner rather than spread evenly over 27.5 years.
- Adding an ADU generally increases your property's assessed value, which can mean a higher property tax bill going forward.

If you're planning to rent out your ADU, the tax side of the equation matters just as much as the construction cost. Here's a general overview of how it typically works, though this is genuinely an area where you want a CPA's eyes on your specific situation before making decisions.

#### Rental Income Is Taxable

Rent you collect from an ADU tenant is taxable income, reported similarly to any other residential rental property. The upside is that, as a rental, the ADU also becomes eligible for the deductions and depreciation available to rental property owners generally.

#### Depreciation: The 27.5-Year Rule

Residential rental property is generally depreciated over 27.5 years under the standard MACRS schedule. A detached ADU (a true backyard cottage or converted detached garage, physically separate from the main house) is typically treated as its own residential rental property and depreciated on that 27.5-year schedule.

Attached ADUs, like an internal conversion or an addition sharing a wall or roofline with the main house, can be more complicated. The IRS generally requires that at least 80% of a building's gross rental income come from dwelling units for it to qualify for the same residential rental treatment, which can affect how an attached unit is classified if you also live in the primary home.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### Accelerated Depreciation Through Cost Segregation

Some ADU owners use a cost segregation study to reclassify certain components of construction cost (specific finishes, fixtures, or systems) into shorter depreciation categories, allowing a larger deduction sooner rather than spread evenly over 27.5 years. With 100% bonus depreciation restored under recent federal tax legislation, a meaningful share of a typical ADU's construction cost can potentially qualify for this kind of accelerated, first-year treatment. This is a specialized strategy that requires a professional cost segregation study to execute correctly, it's not a DIY spreadsheet exercise.

#### Passive Loss Limitations

If your rental produces a paper loss (common in early years once depreciation is factored in), there are limits on how much of that loss you can deduct against your other income, particularly once your modified adjusted gross income rises above roughly $150,000. Below certain income thresholds, more of that loss may be usable; above them, it may be limited or carried forward instead.

#### Property Tax Reassessment

Adding an ADU generally increases your property's assessed value, which can mean a higher property tax bill going forward. This is a real, recurring cost worth factoring into your rental income math from day one, not something to be surprised by after your first post-construction assessment notice arrives.

This article is for general education only and isn't tax advice. Depreciation schedules, passive loss rules, and cost segregation strategies depend heavily on your specific income, ownership structure, and the details of your ADU — talk to a CPA or tax professional before making decisions based on any of the above.

We can't advise you on your taxes, but we can give you accurate, specific construction cost documentation and a clear breakdown of attached vs. detached classification for your unit, which is exactly the information your CPA will need to do this analysis properly.

For the non-tax side of becoming a landlord — deposits, notice periods, and lease basics — see Renting Out Your ADU in Utah: A Landlord's Basics.

## ADU Utility Hookups: Water, Sewer, Electric & Gas Explained
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-adu-utility-hookups.html

ADU Guide

### ADU Utility Hookups: Water, Sewer, Electric & Gas Explained

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Most Utah ADUs tie into the primary home's existing water and sewer lines rather than requiring a brand-new connection to the city main, which keeps costs down substantially compared to a standalone lot.
- Most ADUs run off a new sub-panel fed from the primary home's existing electrical service, provided that service has enough remaining capacity.
- If your ADU includes gas appliances (a furnace, water heater, or range), the gas line typically extends from the existing service line, similar to the electrical approach.
- The single biggest cost factor across all three utilities is distance: how far the ADU sits from the existing hookup points on your property.

Utility hookups are one of the least visible parts of an ADU build, and one of the biggest hidden cost swings between projects. Here's how each system typically works.

#### Water & Sewer: Shared or Separate?

Most Utah ADUs tie into the primary home's existing water and sewer lines rather than requiring a brand-new connection to the city main, which keeps costs down substantially compared to a standalone lot. Whether your city requires a separate water meter for the ADU (common if you plan to rent it out and want to bill tenants directly for usage) versus sharing the primary home's meter is a city-specific and sometimes lot-specific question we confirm during your site visit.

#### Electrical: Sub-Panel vs. Separate Meter

Most ADUs run off a new sub-panel fed from the primary home's existing electrical service, provided that service has enough remaining capacity. If your existing panel is older or already near capacity, a service upgrade may be required before the ADU's sub-panel can be added, which is an added cost worth knowing about early rather than discovering mid-construction. Some homeowners planning to rent the unit long-term opt for a fully separate meter so utility billing is cleanly split between units; this typically costs more upfront but simplifies tenant billing later.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### Gas Line Considerations

If your ADU includes gas appliances (a furnace, water heater, or range), the gas line typically extends from the existing service line, similar to the electrical approach. Detached ADUs generally require a trenched line run underground from the main house or meter to the new structure, which adds both cost and, in colder months, a dependency on ground conditions and frost depth for trenching.

#### What Actually Drives the Cost

The single biggest cost factor across all three utilities is distance: how far the ADU sits from the existing hookup points on your property. A garage conversion sitting right next to the house is the cheapest scenario since utility runs are short. A detached ADU at the back of a deep lot means longer trenching for water, sewer, gas, and electrical conduit, which adds real cost regardless of how simple the rest of the build is.

Existing capacity is the second factor. An older home with a 100-amp electrical panel already near its load limit, or a sewer lateral that's aging or undersized, may need upgrades before the ADU can even be added, and those upgrades benefit the main house too, not just the new unit.

#### How We Handle This

Utility planning happens during your free site visit and design phase, before you're committed to a number. We coordinate directly with utility providers and the city on service capacity, trenching requirements, and meter setups, so utility costs show up as a clear line item in your estimate rather than a surprise change order mid-build. For a full picture of how utility costs fit into overall project budgets, see our ADU cost breakdown.

## The Best Time of Year to Build an ADU in Utah
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-best-time-of-year-to-build-adu-utah.html

ADU Guide

### The Best Time of Year to Build an ADU in Utah

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Permitting doesn't require good weather — submitting your application and working through plan review during the winter months means you're ready to break ground the moment the ground thaws.
- Spring (roughly April through June) tends to offer the best combination of thawed ground, moderate temperatures for concrete curing, and manageable precipitation.
- Once a structure is framed, roofed, and weathered-in, interior work can proceed through the winter months without significant slowdown.
- The best sequence: begin permitting in the off-season, target a spring or early-summer groundbreaking, and aim to have your structure weathered-in before the first real winter storms.

Utah's real winters and hot summers genuinely affect ADU construction timelines, more than homeowners in milder climates typically have to think about. Here's how to time your project so weather works for you instead of against you.

#### Why Timing Matters in a Four-Season State

Concrete work, exterior framing, and roofing all move faster and more predictably in moderate weather. Winter along the Wasatch Front brings frozen ground, snow removal delays, and slower concrete cure times; peak summer brings its own challenges with crew scheduling and material availability during the busiest building season of the year. Neither makes a project impossible, but both affect your timeline and, in some cases, your cost.

#### Start Permitting in Winter

Here's the move most homeowners miss: permitting doesn't require good weather. Submitting your application and working through plan review during the winter months means you're ready to break ground the moment the ground thaws and weather turns favorable, rather than losing weeks of good building weather to a permit that's still sitting in review. If you're thinking about a spring or summer start, the smartest time to have your first site visit and design conversation is actually the preceding fall or winter.

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### Foundation and Framing: The Spring Advantage

Foundation pours and framing are the two phases most sensitive to weather. Spring (roughly April through June) tends to offer the best combination of thawed ground, moderate temperatures for concrete curing, and manageable precipitation compared to Utah's snowier winter months or its occasional intense summer storms. A project that breaks ground in spring is generally on the most predictable path toward a fall move-in.

#### Interior Work Is Largely Winter-Proof

Once a structure is framed, roofed, and weathered-in, interior work (electrical, plumbing, insulation, drywall, flooring, finishes) is far less weather-dependent and can proceed through the winter months without significant slowdown. This is why a project that gets its foundation and framing done before winter can still finish on a reasonable timeline even if final move-in lands in the colder months.

#### A Realistic Month-by-Month Overview

SeasonWhat's Happening

 | Winter (Dec-Feb) | Best time to start permitting and design; slower for foundation/framing

 | Spring (Mar-May) | Ideal window to break ground once permits are issued

 | Summer (Jun-Aug) | Peak construction season; book crews early, it's everyone's busy season

 | Fall (Sep-Nov) | Good window to close in a structure before winter weather arrives

#### The Bottom Line

There isn't a single "best" month to start an ADU in Utah, there's a best sequence: begin permitting in the off-season, target a spring or early-summer groundbreaking, and aim to have your structure framed and weathered-in before the first real winter storms. See our full permitting timeline breakdown for how long each stage typically takes, so you can work backward from your ideal move-in date.

## 7 Common ADU Mistakes Utah Homeowners Make (and How to Avoid Them)
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-common-adu-mistakes.html

ADU Guide

### 7 Common ADU Mistakes Utah Homeowners Make (and How to Avoid Them)

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- An unpermitted structure isn't a shortcut, it's a liability that follows the property.
- Homeowners often budget for the visible construction and forget that trenching water, sewer, gas, and electrical service to a detached unit at the back of the lot can add real cost, especially on deeper lots or older homes with limited electrical capacity.
- The lowest bid is sometimes lowest because corners are being cut on insurance, licensing, or crew experience.

After years of leading ADU projects across the Wasatch Front, the same handful of mistakes show up again and again, almost always because a homeowner moved too fast on the exciting part (design) before locking down the boring part (zoning, budget, and paperwork). Here's what to watch for.

#### 1. Falling in Love With a Design Before Checking Zoning

It's tempting to pick a floor plan first and figure out the rules later. In practice, your lot's size, setbacks, and city-specific size cap should shape the design, not the other way around. A 960 sq ft plan is wasted effort if your city caps detached ADUs at 800 sq ft. Get the zoning check done first, always.

#### 2. Building Without Permits

An unpermitted structure isn't a shortcut, it's a liability that follows the property. It can block financing at resale, void insurance claims, and in some cases require the unit to be brought up to code or removed entirely before a sale can close. Every dollar "saved" by skipping permits tends to cost far more later.

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### 3. Underestimating Utility Hookup Costs

Homeowners often budget for the visible construction and forget that trenching water, sewer, gas, and electrical service to a detached unit at the back of the lot can add real cost, especially on deeper lots or older homes with limited electrical capacity. See our utility hookup guide for what typically drives this cost up or down.

#### 4. Choosing the Cheapest Bid Without Checking License and Insurance

The lowest bid is sometimes lowest because corners are being cut on insurance, licensing, or crew experience. Always verify a Utah GC license directly through DOPL and ask for proof of insurance before signing anything, regardless of how competitive the price looks. Our full builder-vetting checklist covers this in detail.

#### 5. Ignoring Parking Requirements

Several Utah cities require an additional off-street parking space for an ADU, and depending on your lot's existing driveway and setbacks, that can be a real design constraint, not a formality. This is exactly the kind of detail that should come up during your initial site visit, not after plans are finalized.

#### 6. Designing for Today's Family, Not Tomorrow's Market

An oddly-laid-out unit built purely around one family's current needs can be harder to rent or resell later. Standard, functional layouts (a real bedroom, a full kitchen, in-unit or accessible laundry) tend to hold rental and resale value better than highly customized one-off designs, even if the customized version feels perfect for right now.

#### 7. No Contingency Line Item in the Budget

Older homes especially can hide surprises once walls are opened or foundations are excavated. Budgeting a contingency of roughly 10% on top of your expected project cost is standard practice, and it's far better to not need it than to be caught without one.

None of these mistakes are complicated to avoid, they just require slowing down at the start. That's the entire purpose of a proper free site visit: catching zoning issues, utility realities, and design tradeoffs before you're financially committed to a plan that doesn't actually fit your lot.

## Does an ADU Increase Your Property Value? What the Data Shows
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-does-an-adu-increase-property-value.html

ADU Guide

### Does an ADU Increase Your Property Value? What the Data Shows

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Across recent national studies, homes with a legally built ADU tend to sell for meaningfully more than comparable homes without one, with industry data citing increases in the broad range of 20-35% depending on the market.
- This is worth repeating because it matters more than any other variable: an unpermitted ADU can actively hurt your home's value instead of helping it.
- Appraisal standards for ADUs have gotten more consistent recently, with updated appraisal datasets giving appraisers clearer guidance on how to document a second unit's contribution to value.

Every homeowner considering an ADU eventually asks some version of the same question: is this actually going to be worth it? The honest answer is that it depends heavily on one thing more than any other — whether the unit is permitted. But let's start with what the broader data actually shows.

#### What National Data Shows

Across recent national studies, homes with a legally built ADU tend to sell for meaningfully more than comparable homes without one, with industry data citing increases in the broad range of 20-35% depending on the market. The National Association of Realtors has cited figures on the higher end of that range nationally, though markets with a more mature ADU culture (much of California, for example) tend to see the strongest and best-documented gains, since buyers there are more used to placing a dollar value on a rentable second unit.

Utah-specific data is thinner simply because ADUs are newer here than in states that have allowed them for decades. But the underlying logic — a legal second unit that can generate rental income or house family adds real, appraisable value — applies just as much along the Wasatch Front as anywhere else.

#### Why ADUs Add Value in Utah Specifically

Two Utah-specific forces make ADUs particularly valuable here right now. First, the Wasatch Front has a genuine housing shortage, which means rental demand for a well-built ADU is strong in Salt Lake City, Provo, Ogden, and Park City alike. Second, multigenerational living has become increasingly common as home prices have climbed, and a private, code-compliant unit for aging parents or adult children is a feature buyers are actively searching for, not just tolerating.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### The Single Biggest Factor: Permitted vs. Unpermitted

This is worth repeating because it matters more than any other variable: an unpermitted ADU can actively hurt your home's value instead of helping it. Appraisers can't credit square footage or income potential they can't verify against city records, buyers' lenders may refuse to finance a purchase once an unpermitted structure is discovered, and you may be required to bring the unit up to code (or remove it) before you can sell at all. Every estimate we give includes full permitting as standard — it's not an upsell, it's the only way the added value is real and defensible.

#### How Appraisers Actually Evaluate an ADU

Appraisal standards for ADUs have gotten more consistent recently, with updated appraisal datasets giving appraisers clearer guidance on how to document a second unit's contribution to value. In practice, an appraiser will typically weigh three things: comparable sales of similar properties with ADUs in your area, the unit's demonstrated or reasonably projected rental income, and the actual construction cost, particularly for higher-end custom builds.

#### What This Means If You're Deciding Whether to Build

If your primary goal is resale value, a permitted ADU is a legitimately strong investment in most Utah markets right now, but it isn't a guaranteed dollar-for-dollar return, and value gains vary by neighborhood, unit quality, and local rental demand. If your primary goal is rental income or housing family, the value question becomes secondary to whether the unit pays for itself — see our financing overview for how most Utah homeowners fund the build, and our cost breakdown for what to budget.

Either way, get a professional opinion specific to your property before treating any of these figures as a guarantee — a local appraiser or real estate agent familiar with ADUs in your specific neighborhood can give you a far more precise number than any national statistic.

## Garage Conversion ADU: What's Really Involved (Cost, Code, Timeline)
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-garage-conversion-adu-guide.html

ADU Guide

### Garage Conversion ADU: What's Really Involved (Cost, Code, Timeline)

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Before any conversion work starts, we assess the garage's existing foundation, framing, and roof structure.
- Building code requires habitable rooms to have a minimum finished ceiling height of 7 feet across at least half the room's floor area, with a reduced 6'8" minimum allowed in bathrooms and similar spaces.
- Any room used as a sleeping area needs a code-compliant emergency egress opening: a minimum 20 inches wide, 24 inches tall, at least 5.7 square feet of net clear opening, with a sill no higher than 44 inches above the floor.

A garage conversion is usually the fastest, most affordable path to an ADU in Utah, but "convert the garage" undersells how much actual construction work is involved in turning an unheated storage space into a fully legal, code-compliant home.

#### Structural Assessment First

Before any conversion work starts, we assess the garage's existing foundation, framing, and roof structure. Most garage slabs weren't poured to residential living-space standards, and framing sized for a garage door opening often needs reinforcement once that opening is closed in and load paths change. This assessment determines how much of the existing structure can stay versus what needs to be rebuilt.

#### Ceiling Height Requirements

Building code requires habitable rooms to have a minimum finished ceiling height of 7 feet across at least half the room's floor area, with a reduced 6'8" minimum allowed in bathrooms and similar spaces. Many garages were built with lower ceiling heights than this, especially older ones, which can mean adjusting the roof structure or excavating the slab, both of which add cost and complexity beyond simply insulating and drywalling.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### Egress Window Requirements

Any room used as a sleeping area needs a code-compliant emergency egress opening: a minimum 20 inches wide, 24 inches tall, at least 5.7 square feet of net clear opening, with a sill no higher than 44 inches above the floor. A code-compliant exterior door (at least 32 inches wide and 78 inches tall) can also satisfy this in some layouts. Garages typically have a single large garage-door opening and maybe one small side window, neither of which meets egress requirements as-is, so cutting a new, properly sized window opening into the wall is standard scope on almost every garage conversion.

#### Insulation: The Biggest Practical Difference

A garage is built to store cars, not to be comfortable to live in. Garage conversions require full wall, ceiling, and often slab insulation upgrades to meet residential energy code, plus proper vapor barriers and air sealing. Skipping or underbuilding this step is the single most common reason a converted garage feels noticeably colder or hotter than the rest of the house after the work is "done."

#### Utility Hookups

Because a garage is typically attached to or very close to the main house, utility runs for water, sewer, gas, and electrical are usually short and relatively affordable compared to a detached backyard ADU — see our full utility hookup guide for how each system typically connects.

#### Realistic Cost and Timeline

Garage conversions typically run $50,000-$120,000 depending on the scope of structural, ceiling height, and insulation work required, and take about 2-3 months from permit approval to completion — the fastest of the three ADU types we build. See our full cost breakdown by ADU type for how this compares to modular and custom stickbuilt options.

The properties where a garage conversion works best have decent existing ceiling height, a garage close to existing utility hookups, and structure that doesn't need a full rebuild. We'll tell you honestly during your free site visit if your garage is a great candidate or if a different ADU type would actually save you money.

One upside worth knowing if you're in an HOA: an attached garage conversion is typically treated as an internal ADU, which HOAs have much less power to block than a detached backyard unit. See Can Your HOA Stop You From Building an ADU in Utah? for the distinction.

## HELOC vs. Construction Loan: How to Finance Your Utah ADU
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-heloc-vs-construction-loan-adu-financing.html

ADU Guide

### HELOC vs. Construction Loan: How to Finance Your Utah ADU

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- A HELOC works like a credit card backed by your home's equity.
- A construction loan is purpose-built for projects like this — funds release in stages as construction milestones are hit, and some lenders now offer ADU-specific products with streamlined approval for projects under $250,000.
- If you already have significant equity in your home and want flexibility to draw funds as you go, a HELOC is usually the simpler, cheaper option.

Most homeowners don't pay cash for an ADU — they finance it, usually using equity they've already built up in their home. Two options come up most often: a HELOC and a construction loan. Here's the short version of how each works.

#### HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit)

A HELOC works like a credit card backed by your home's equity. You're approved for a credit limit and draw funds as you need them during construction, paying interest only on what you actually use. Rates are typically variable (prime plus 0 to 2%), with a draw period of 5 to 10 years. Most lenders let you borrow up to 85% of your home's equity. It's the most popular option because of its flexibility, especially for phased projects.

#### Construction Loan / ADU Loan

A construction loan is purpose-built for projects like this — funds release in stages as construction milestones are hit, and some lenders now offer ADU-specific products with streamlined approval for projects under $250,000. Rates run slightly higher than a standard mortgage during the construction phase, and it typically converts to a permanent loan once the build is finished. This is often the right fit if you don't have much existing equity to draw against.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### A Quick Way to Think About It

If you already have significant equity in your home and want flexibility to draw funds as you go, a HELOC is usually the simpler, cheaper option. If your equity is limited or you'd rather have funds tied directly to construction milestones, a construction loan is worth a closer look. There are also home equity loans (a fixed lump sum instead of a credit line) and cash-out refinances, which make sense in different situations.

For a full comparison — including a worked example of how lenders calculate what you can borrow, and what to do before you apply — see our complete ADU Financing Guide.
