## How Much Does an ADU Cost in Utah? 2026 Price Breakdown
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-how-much-does-an-adu-cost-in-utah.html

ADU Guide

### How Much Does an ADU Cost in Utah? 2026 Price Breakdown

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Garage conversion ADUs typically run $50,000 – $120,000.
- Modular / prefab ADUs typically run $120,000 – $200,000.
- Custom stickbuilt ADUs typically run $120,000 – $300,000.
- Utah ADUs are renting for roughly $1,200 to $2,500 a month depending on size, location, and finishes — strongest in markets like Salt Lake City and Park City.

The honest answer is "it depends" — but that's not very useful when you're trying to plan a budget. Here are the real ranges we're seeing on Utah ADU projects in 2026, broken down by build type, plus the factors that move a project from the low end to the high end.

#### Cost by Build Type

Garage Conversion ADU: $50,000 – $120,000. The most affordable path, since you're working with an existing structure and skipping foundation and framing costs. Best for homeowners who already have a usable garage and want rental income without a large upfront investment.

Prefab / Modular ADU: $120,000 – $200,000. Factory-built and assembled on your lot. Faster to complete (typically 50 to 70% faster than a traditional build) and generally more cost-effective than a full custom build, while still meeting the same code standards.

Custom Stickbuilt ADU: $120,000 – $300,000. Built on-site from the ground up with full design flexibility. The highest ceiling on finishes and customization, and typically the highest long-term property value and rental appeal.

See our full ADU Pricing Guide for a detailed cost breakdown, or browse specific floor plans and starting prices.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### What Actually Moves the Price

- Size. Bigger units cost more in total, but the cost per square foot actually goes down as the unit gets larger.

- Site prep. Sloped lots, poor soil, or difficult access add cost. Flat, accessible lots with nearby utility connections are cheaper to build on.

- Finishes. Standard finishes are included in base pricing; upgraded flooring, custom cabinetry, and premium fixtures can add $10,000 to $40,000.

- Permits. City permit fees in Utah typically run $3,000 to $12,000 depending on the municipality — and every city's process is a little different (see our Utah ADU law breakdown).

- Utility connections. Water, sewer, gas, and electrical hookups vary significantly based on distance from your main home and existing infrastructure.

#### What Kind of Return Should You Expect?

Utah ADUs are renting for roughly $1,200 to $2,500 a month depending on size, location, and finishes — strongest in markets like Salt Lake City and Park City. Most owners recoup their full investment through rental income within 5 to 10 years, and a finished, permitted ADU can add 20 to 30% to your home's value on top of the rental income.

These are ranges, not quotes. The only way to get an accurate number for your specific property is a free site visit — we'll walk your lot and give you a straight number, no pressure.

## How to Choose an ADU Builder in Utah: A 10-Point Checklist
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-how-to-choose-an-adu-builder.html

ADU Guide

### How to Choose an ADU Builder in Utah: A 10-Point Checklist

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 31, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Ask for the license number directly and look it up yourself through the Utah Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL).
- General liability insurance protects you if something goes wrong on your property during construction.

An ADU is a major project, often the largest single home investment a homeowner will make after buying the house itself. The builder you choose matters more than almost any other decision in the process. Here's what to actually check.

#### 1. A Real, Verifiable Utah General Contractor License

Ask for the license number directly and look it up yourself through the Utah Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL). A legitimate builder will give you this without hesitation. For reference, ours is Utah GC License #14296577-5501.

#### 2. Proof of Insurance and Bonding

General liability insurance protects you if something goes wrong on your property during construction. Ask for a certificate of insurance, not just a verbal assurance.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### 3. A Real Portfolio of Local, Completed Projects

Renderings and stock photos are easy to produce. Ask specifically for photos of projects the builder has personally completed in Utah, ideally ones you can drive by. Our gallery shows completed work, not just concept renderings.

#### 4. Who Actually Manages Your Project

Some companies sell the job, then hand it off entirely to subcontractors you never meet. Ask directly: who will be on-site managing this day to day, and how much of the actual construction work is subcontracted out? Neither answer is automatically wrong, but you deserve to know it upfront.

#### 5. Contract Structure: Fixed Price vs. Cost-Plus

Understand exactly what you're signing. A fixed-price (lump sum) contract gives you cost certainty upfront. A cost-plus contract can offer more flexibility on selections but requires more trust and clearer reporting on actual costs. Neither is a red flag by itself — a vague contract that doesn't specify which one you have, is.

#### 6. Permitting and Inspections Included, Not Billed as an Extra

Confirm in writing that permit applications, plan revisions, and every required inspection are handled by the builder as part of the scope, not passed back to you or billed piecemeal later.

#### 7. A Realistic Timeline, Not an Aspirational One

Be skeptical of a builder who promises a custom stickbuilt ADU in 6 weeks. Realistic ranges in Utah run 2-3 months for a garage conversion, 3-5 months for modular, and 5-8 months for custom stickbuilt, and that's after permitting is complete. See our full cost and timeline breakdown.

#### 8. Willingness to Provide References

Ask to speak with two or three past clients directly, not just read testimonials on a website. A builder confident in their work will connect you without hesitation.

#### 9. Clear, Responsive Communication From the First Call

How a builder communicates during the sales process is usually a preview of how they'll communicate during construction. Slow replies and vague answers now rarely improve once you've signed.

#### 10. A Contract That Spells Out Draws, Change Orders, and Selections

Payment draw schedules, how change orders get priced and approved, and what's included vs. considered an upgrade should all be explicit in writing before you sign anything.

If you want a second opinion or just want to compare notes against a specific proposal you've already received, we're happy to talk through it during a free, no-obligation site visit.

## Modular vs. Stickbuilt ADU: Which Is Right for Your Utah Property?
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-modular-vs-stickbuilt-adu.html

ADU Guide

### Modular vs. Stickbuilt ADU: Which Is Right for Your Utah Property?

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- A modular ADU is built in a factory, then delivered and assembled on your lot on a foundation.
- A stickbuilt ADU is framed and built entirely on-site, the same way most houses are built.
- If you want the fastest path to a finished, permitted ADU at a lower cost, modular is usually the better fit.

One of the first decisions in any ADU project isn't which floor plan you like — it's whether to go modular or stickbuilt. Both are built to the same Utah code and go through the same permitting and inspection process. The difference is in how they're built, and what that means for your cost, timeline, and end result.

#### Modular / Prefab ADU

A modular ADU is built in a factory, then delivered and assembled on your lot on a foundation. Because it's built indoors on an assembly line, it's typically 50 to 70% faster than a traditional build — often 3 to 5 months from permit approval to move-in. Labor costs are lower, which generally makes modular the more budget-friendly option at $120,000 to $200,000. You're choosing from a set of pre-designed floor plans rather than starting from a blank page, but those plans still cover a range of layouts from studios to two-bedroom units.

#### Custom Stickbuilt ADU

A stickbuilt ADU is framed and built entirely on-site, the same way most houses are built. That means full design flexibility — your floor plan, your finishes, and a design that can be matched to your existing home's architecture. It's the better choice if you want something studio-to-3-bedroom sized and fully tailored to your lot, but it takes longer (typically 5 to 8 months) and costs more, from $120,000 up to $300,000 depending on size and finishes.

💲

What would an ADU cost on your property? Get an instant ballpark for a garage conversion, modular, or custom ADU, based on real Utah project pricing.Try the Cost Calculator →

#### Quick Comparison

 ModularStickbuilt

 | Typical Cost | $120K – $200K | $120K – $300K

 | Typical Timeline | 3 – 5 months | 5 – 8 months

 | Customization | Choose from set floor plans | Fully custom design

 | Best For | Speed and value | Maximum flexibility & long-term value

#### Which Should You Choose?

If you want the fastest path to a finished, permitted ADU at a lower cost, modular is usually the better fit. If your priority is matching your home's exact architecture, maximizing bedrooms and layout for your specific lot, or you're building toward the highest possible long-term property value, stickbuilt is worth the extra time and cost.

Browse our specific modular and stickbuilt floor plans, or get a free site visit and we'll help you figure out which build type actually makes sense for your lot and goals.

## Renting Out Your ADU in Utah: A Landlord's Basics
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-renting-out-adu-landlord-basics-utah.html

ADU Guide

### Renting Out Your ADU in Utah: A Landlord's Basics

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published August 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- Utah doesn't cap how much you can charge for a security deposit — that's between you and your tenant.
- Utah requires landlords to give tenants the name and address of the property owner, plus anyone authorized to manage the property or accept legal notices on the owner's behalf.

Building the ADU is phase one. Renting it out is phase two — and that's where a lot of first-time landlords in Utah get tripped up, not because the rules are complicated, but because nobody hands you a checklist. Here's the short version of what Utah law actually requires.

#### Security Deposits

Utah doesn't cap how much you can charge for a security deposit — that's between you and your tenant. What the law does require is that you return it, along with an itemized list of any deductions, within 30 days of the tenant moving out. Miss that window without a valid reason, and a tenant can sue you for the deposit plus an additional $100.

#### Notice Periods You Need to Know

If you're renting month-to-month (the most common setup for an ADU), three notice periods matter:

- Raising the rent: at least 15 days' written notice before the increase takes effect

- Ending the tenancy: at least 15 days' written notice, from either side

- Nonpayment of rent: a 3-day notice to pay or vacate before you can file for eviction

A fixed-term lease changes some of this — notice requirements for ending a lease early or non-renewal can differ from the month-to-month defaults above, so it's worth having your lease reviewed if you're using anything other than a standard month-to-month agreement.

📐

Wondering if your lot qualifies? Utah's new 2026 law opened up detached ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft in most cities. Answer 6 quick questions and see your options.Check My Lot Free →

#### The Disclosure Most Landlords Miss

Utah requires landlords to give tenants the name and address of the property owner, plus anyone authorized to manage the property or accept legal notices on the owner's behalf. It's an easy line to forget, but it's just as easy to include — most standard Utah lease templates already have a field for it. If you're self-managing, that's simply your own name and mailing address.

#### Where This Connects to Insurance and Taxes

Notice periods and deposits are the day-to-day mechanics, but renting out an ADU also touches your insurance coverage and your tax return. We cover those separately: see ADU Insurance: What Utah Homeowners Need to Know and ADU Tax Implications for the financial side of becoming a landlord.

This is a general summary of common Utah landlord-tenant requirements, not legal advice, and it isn't exhaustive — local ordinances, HOA rules, and your specific lease terms can add requirements on top of state law. Have a local attorney or property manager review your lease before you sign your first tenant.

## Is an ADU Legal in Utah? HB82, SB284, and What's Changed
URL: https://utahbackyardadus.com/blog-utah-adu-laws-hb82-sb284-explained.html

ADU Guide

### Is an ADU Legal in Utah? HB82, SB284, and What's Changed

By Sam Lewis, Licensed Utah General Contractor · Published July 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

 ← Back to all guides

#### Key takeaways

- In 2021, Utah passed HB82, which requires most cities in the state to allow accessory dwelling units on single-family lots — meaning a city generally can't ban ADUs outright.
- Utah's legislature followed up in 2026 with SB284, which requires most larger Utah cities to permit detached ADUs on single-family lots of 11,000 sq ft or more, starting October 1, 2026.

🆕

Updated for Oct. 1, 2026: SB284 now requires most Utah cities to allow detached backyard ADUs on lots 11,000+ sq ft, with capped parking and no conditional use permit.Read the full SB284 breakdown →

If you've searched "can I build an ADU in Utah," you've probably run into conflicting answers — some pages talk about a 2021 law, others mention new rules for 2026. Here's what's actually true, in plain English.

#### HB82 (2021): The Law That Opened the Door

In 2021, Utah passed HB82, which requires most cities in the state to allow accessory dwelling units on single-family lots — meaning a city generally can't ban ADUs outright. HB82 doesn't impose a single statewide owner-occupancy rule, but it lets cities prohibit renting an internal ADU in a home that isn't the owner's primary residence, and SB284 (2026) lets cities require the owner to live in either the house or a detached ADU.

The key word is "in theory." HB82 set a statewide floor, but it left cities in control of the details: size limits, setbacks, parking requirements, and design standards. Many cities use that authority — Salt Lake City, Provo, and Ogden all require owner occupancy today. We cover each city's specifics on our Salt Lake City, Provo, and Ogden ADU pages.

#### SB284 (2026): Detached ADUs Get a Bigger Push

Utah's legislature followed up in 2026 with SB284, which requires most larger Utah cities (first- through fourth-class cities, plus fifth-class cities of 5,000+ in larger counties) to permit detached ADUs as a permitted use on single-family lots of 11,000 sq ft or more, starting October 1, 2026. Cities that don't already have a compliant ADU ordinance are required to adopt one by October 2026.

This matters most in cities that historically limited ADUs to a specific overlay zone or to attached/internal units only. Provo is a good example: it had an ADU overlay that didn't cover the whole city, and SB284 is expanding where a detached ADU is allowed. Park City is seeing something similar, with larger lots (roughly 11,000+ sq ft) now having a clearer path to a detached unit.

#### So What Does This Mean for You?

Two things are true at the same time in Utah right now:

- State law is on your side. Between HB82 and SB284, the trend has been consistently toward making ADUs easier to build, not harder.

- Your city still controls the details. Size caps, parking, setbacks, and (in some cities) owner-occupancy are all set locally, and they vary a lot — Ogden caps detached ADUs at 800 sq ft, Salt Lake City allows up to 1,000 sq ft, and Park City's limit depends on your primary home's size.

Laws and ordinances change, and every lot is different. The only way to know exactly what your property qualifies for is to have someone check your specific zoning — which is exactly what we do during your free site visit, at no cost.

One thing state law doesn't override: your HOA, if you have one. See Can Your HOA Stop You From Building an ADU in Utah? for how that works.
